Appendix E Training Details

Training corpus.

The canonical training corpus is a four-domain extractive MCQ dataset covering Financial filings, Project Gutenberg literature, Legal documents, and Code. Each item is structured as

(ctx_ids, prompt_ids, answer_ids),\texttt{(ctx\_ids, prompt\_ids, answer\_ids)},

with ctx_ids the long-context prefill, prompt_ids the MCQ question, and answer_ids the answer-letter target. Questions are constructed from random 11k-token sub-chunks of the prefill, verified by the same frozen base model used as teacher, and filtered to remove items the base model can answer without the context.

For the canonical 88k-context Qwen3-4B run, raw per-domain item counts are:

Domain Items
Financial 236,808236{,}808
Project Gutenberg 110,567110{,}567
Code 38,39438{,}394
Legal 30,13630{,}136
Capped per-domain (training) 30,13630{,}136
Total training items 120,544120{,}544

Domains are downsampled to the smallest, giving roughly 1.01.0B context tokens at 88k context length before prompt and answer tokens.

Loss details.

The training signal is forward KL from the full-context teacher to the compact-cache student, evaluated only on answer-side tokens. The KL is computed against the top-200200 teacher-vocabulary tokens with the gold answer token forced into the support; this keeps the per-step memory cost bounded. Appendix F reports a small retraining ablation showing that top-200200 is not worse than top-10001000 or full-vocabulary support under a common full-vocabulary evaluation. Prompt and pad tokens are masked out of the loss.

Optimization.

Optimizer AdamW, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95
Learning rate 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}
Warmup 100100 steps, linear from 10−610^{-6}
Schedule Constant after warmup
Weight decay 0.010.01 on matrix params, 00 on biases / 1D params
Gradient clipping 1.01.0
Microbatch 44 per GPU
GPUs 8×8\times NVIDIA H200 (DDP)
Gradient accumulation 11
Effective batch 3232
Headline checkpoint step 15001500

The compactor parameters are the only trainable parameters; base-model weights are frozen throughout. Except for the explicitly labeled generation-aligned LongBench checkpoint in §3.5, paper-facing Qwen3-4B Still numbers use the step-15001500 checkpoint. The above refers to 256 latents on 32k sequence length.

Compute accounting.

All reported training and evaluation jobs were run on managed cloud GPU workers. The main Qwen3-4B Still and KV-Distill checkpoints use 8×8\times NVIDIA H200 workers (141GB HBM per GPU). Architecture, factorization, and latent-count ablations use the same step-15001500 cutoff and the same class of workers; some replacement runs use 4×4\times H200 workers with adjusted microbatching to keep the effective batch at 3232. Scale-transfer runs use H200 workers with model-specific microbatch and gradient-checkpointing settings. The Still, KV-Distill, H2O, SnapKV, StreamingLLM, HELMET, RULER, LongBench, and summarization evaluations use one to four H100/H200 workers depending on model size and context length. The paper-facing numbers exclude preliminary failed or diagnostic jobs, which required additional exploratory compute beyond this reproduction budget.

Iterative Compaction

To implement iteration, we train over multiple passes using the same compactor at each pass. We found that a reduced learning rate of 2e-4 was necessary in this setting. The Lookahead optimizer [Zhang et al., 2019] improves training stability. Alternatively, competitive results can be achieved without Lookahead by adding an auxiliary loss at every prefill.

For the aux-KV iterative variant, we optimize a joint objective:

ℒ=ℒMCQ+λaux​ℒaux-kv,λaux=0.5.\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{MCQ}}+\lambda_{\text{aux}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux-kv}},\qquad\lambda_{\text{aux}}=0.5. (12)

The auxiliary term is computed on all passes except the first, by matching student chunk K/V against teacher full-prefill chunk K/V. For each pass pp and layer ℓ\ell, we compute normalized relative errors

rp,ℓ(K)=mean⁡((Ks−Kt)2)max⁡(mean⁡(Kt2),ϵ),rp,ℓ(V)=mean⁡((Vs−Vt)2)max⁡(mean⁡(Vt2),ϵ),ϵ=1​e−8r^{(K)}_{p,\ell}=\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{mean}\!\left((K_{s}-K_{t})^{2}\right)}{\max\!\left(\operatorname{mean}(K_{t}^{2}),\,\epsilon\right)}},\qquad r^{(V)}_{p,\ell}=\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{mean}\!\left((V_{s}-V_{t})^{2}\right)}{\max\!\left(\operatorname{mean}(V_{t}^{2}),\,\epsilon\right)}},\qquad\epsilon=1e-8 (13)

and apply a Huber loss averaged over layers and passes:

ℒaux-kv=∑p=1Nw~p​1L​∑ℓ=1LHuberδ⁡(rp,ℓ(K))+Huberδ⁡(rp,ℓ(V))2,δ=1.0,\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux-kv}}=\sum_{p=1}^{N}\tilde{w}_{p}\,\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\frac{\operatorname{Huber}_{\delta}\!\left(r^{(K)}_{p,\ell}\right)+\operatorname{Huber}_{\delta}\!\left(r^{(V)}_{p,\ell}\right)}{2},\qquad\delta=1.0, (14)

where wp∝(N−p+1)w_{p}\propto(N-p+1), normalized as w~p=wp/∑jwj\tilde{w}_{p}=w_{p}/\sum_{j}w_{j}, so that earlier passes receive larger weight. Empirically, this variant remains competitive through 32k context but does not match the quality of its Lookahead counterpart (Figure 20).

Appendix F Top-kk KL Support Ablation

We check whether the top-200200 teacher-vocabulary support used in the main training loss is an overly aggressive approximation. We retrain four Qwen3-4B Still compactors on the same four-domain MCQ mixture at 44k context length, 512512 latents, and 10001000 steps, varying only the teacher KL support: top-5050, top-200200, top-10001000, or the full vocabulary. We then evaluate all final checkpoints on the same 200200 held-out MCQ examples using full-vocabulary KL and compact-cache cross-entropy.

Appendix G Baseline Implementation Details

This appendix records the exact configuration used for each baseline in §2.5.

H2O [Zhang et al., 2023].

Reference queries are extracted via repeat-prefill on the same prefix, matching the protocol of Zweiger et al. [2026]. Token retention scores are cumulative attention weights from the extracted queries; the top-KK tokens by cumulative score are kept. Values are taken directly from the retained source positions (c2_method=direct) and no β\beta correction is applied. The cache budget KK is varied across experiments to match Still’s compression ratio.

SnapKV [Li et al., 2024].

Token scoring restricts attention to a 6464-token observation window of recent positions, with a 55-token pooling kernel applied to the score vector before top-KK selection. Retained keys and values are taken directly from the source positions; no β\beta correction.

StreamingLLM [Xiao et al., 2024].

The cache consists of 44 attention-sink tokens at the start of the prefix together with the most recent K−4K-4 tokens, for a total budget of KK. Sinks are taken from the absolute first positions of the prefix in the un-rotated cache, matching the construction of Xiao et al. [2024]. No β\beta correction.

Attention Matching [Zweiger et al., 2026].

Reference queries are extracted by re-prefilling the original context through the frozen base model, following Zweiger et al. [2026]. The primary Attention Matching curve uses the highest-attention-keys variant: key selection takes the top-KK source positions by RMS attention score, compact values are reconstructed by least squares against the extracted queries, and the per-token bias β\beta is fitted by bounded nonnegative least squares with two refinement iterations. We also implemented the paper’s Orthogonal Matching Pursuit family, including the batched OMP schedule. The dashed AM-OMP-fast curve in Figure 2 is this diagnostic variant: it is useful for checking the high-quality side of the per-context-synthesis frontier, but it is not uniformly more accurate than the top-KK variant on our Qwen3-4B sweep. The Still–AM cell-level comparison in Appendix J therefore uses the measured top-KK Attention Matching curve.

G.1 KV-Distill fairness and optimization

KV-Distill is trained on Qwen3-4B with the same four-domain corpus and matching context-length splits as Still; we do not use released checkpoints. A learned scorer reads frozen layer-66 hidden states and selects the top-KK tokens, with the first 88 tokens forced as sinks. Rank-128128 LoRA adaptors are attached to Q,K,V,OQ,K,V,O; Q/OQ/O adaptors are applied only to selected tokens and K/VK/V adaptors to the full prefill. The adapted model is run over the full context, the selected K/V rows are sliced from that adapted cache, and the frozen base model then answers against the compressed cache. Training uses symmetric KL distillation (λ=0.6\lambda=0.6) on answer-side tokens plus an auxiliary scorer loss toward key-RMS selection targets. The question/answer path is left uncompressed at inference, matching Still’s evaluation path. The paper-facing checkpoints are taken at step 15001500 for the matched sweeps rather than selected per cell by test accuracy. We note that the loss plateaus for both before 1500 for all configurations.

G.2 Baseline selection and tuning policy

The plotted matrix keeps one configuration per method across tasks and context lengths, with only the cache budget KK varying to match the target compression ratio. This fixed policy avoids per-cell tuning on the evaluation grid, but it is not a default-only implementation pass: we tried the main baseline-strengthening choices in Table 6 and then fixed one paper-facing policy per method.

For heuristic selection baselines, the final policies use the published operating points that define the methods in this setting together with the shared evaluation path. For Attention Matching and KV-Distill, we include the strongest matched variants we implemented under the same Qwen3-4B model family, data mixture, cache budget grid, and uncompressed question/answer continuation path used by Still. The fixed checkpoint policy is also deliberate: paper-facing KV-Distill cells use the matched step-15001500 checkpoint for each run, not the best checkpoint selected by test or validation accuracy.

Additional baselines considered.

PyramidKV appears in the design-space taxonomy because it is an important selection baseline, but it is not included in the reported Qwen3-4B numeric matrix. KVZip [Kim et al., 2025] is closer to Still’s deployment regime because it scores cache entries without knowing the future user query. We therefore add a targeted 8k/16k KVZip comparison under the same Qwen3-4B MCQ protocol as the other frontier baselines; Appendix J.1 gives the implementation details, partial results, and scope rationale. Two recent query-agnostic or learned-eviction methods remain especially relevant for future matched comparisons: Compactor [Chari and Durme, 2025], which uses approximate leverage scores with context calibration and a vLLM-oriented sparse-cache implementation, and KVP [Moschella et al., 2026], which trains lightweight per-head policies to rank tokens for future utility. We do not claim numerical dominance over baselines not run under the shared Qwen3-4B protocol above.

Appendix H Latent Capacity and Context-Length Sweeps

The compactor exposes two scaling knobs at fixed architecture: the latent count tt, which controls compression ratio at a given input length, and the input length TT itself. The single-sentence claim in §3.1 (compact-cache utility rises monotonically with latent count and is mostly stable at fixed compression across context lengths) compresses three sweeps, which we report in detail below. All sweeps use the canonical Qwen3-4B configuration of §2.1 and the multidomain training corpus of §E unless otherwise stated; tail-mean conventions follow the figure captions.

H.1 Latent count at fixed context length

We sweep latent counts t∈{32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048}t\in\{32,64,128,256,512,1024,2048\} at fixed context length T=8192T=8192, training a fresh compactor at each setting under the canonical recipe. Figure 7 reports eight metrics on the single-domain MCQ benchmark. Compact MCQ accuracy rises monotonically with tt, with the steepest gains between 128128 and 10241024 latents and diminishing returns thereafter — the gap between t=1024t=1024 and t=2048t=2048 is small relative to the gap between t=256t=256 and t=1024t=1024. CE utilization tracks compact MCQ accuracy across the entire sweep. This is the basic empirical condition under which the proxy loss Still actually optimizes during training (forward KL on answer-side tokens) and the downstream extractive metric (multiple-choice answer accuracy) move together: optimizing for the proxy is faithful to the deployment objective at every operating point in this regime.

The same sweep on the multidomain corpus (Figure 8) shows the same shape: train loss, eval KL, and eval CE all decrease smoothly with tt; the three utilization definitions all rise toward the full-context ceiling; and compact MCQ accuracy reaches within ∼4\sim 4 points of the full-context baseline at t=1024t=1024 — the canonical 8×8\times compression operating point. The multidomain numbers are slightly lower than single-domain at matched tt, consistent with the multidomain corpus being harder on average, but the qualitative scaling is identical.

The displayed per-domain breakdown (Figure 9) confirms that the aggregate scaling is not a domain-mixing artefact. Financial, Gutenberg, and Legal each scale smoothly with tt and converge above 80%80\% compact accuracy by t=1024t=1024. Code is included in the multidomain corpus used for this sweep; the plotted diagnostic focuses on the three displayed domains for readability rather than changing the training or evaluation mixture.

H.2 Variable-context evaluation at fixed checkpoint

A potential concern with the sweep above is that each (T,t)(T,t) point is a separately trained compactor, and the smooth scaling we observe could be a property of the training distribution rather than of the compactor itself — a checkpoint trained at one context length might collapse on shorter or longer inputs. Figure 10 addresses this directly. We take a single canonical checkpoint — the multidomain 10241024-latent compactor trained at T=8192T=8192 — and evaluate it on held-out MCQs bucketed by document length from 11k to 88k tokens, with no retraining or per-bucket adaptation. Compact accuracy holds up across the full bucket range. This is the basic generalization condition for using a single checkpoint at deployment time, where input lengths vary continuously and per-input retraining is not an option.

We then run a stricter fixed-cache study in which the compact budget is held at t=512t=512 while input length varies over T∈{4​k,8​k,16​k,32​k}T\in\{4\mathrm{k},8\mathrm{k},16\mathrm{k},32\mathrm{k}\} during training and up to 64​k64\mathrm{k} at evaluation. Figure 11 compares per-length specialists to single-length checkpoints and to one mixed-length checkpoint trained with scaled compactor positions and a length/compression embedding. The mixed checkpoint pays a short-context tax relative to specialists at 44k and 88k, but is strongest at the long end, reaching 48.0%48.0\% at 3232k and 44.7%44.7\% at the held-out 6464k point. By contrast, the 88k-only checkpoint reaches 40.7%40.7\% at 3232k but falls to 29.3%29.3\% at 6464k. Thus mixed-TT training gives a useful one-checkpoint deployment point for long inputs, but it does not yet remove the quality cost of length specialization at short contexts.

H.3 Context length at fixed compression ratio

The complementary question is what happens when we hold compression ratio fixed and vary absolute context length. We sweep (T,t)∈{(1​k,128),(2​k,256),(4​k,512),(8​k,1024)}(T,t)\in\{(1\text{k},128),(2\text{k},256),(4\text{k},512),(8\text{k},1024)\}, training a separate compactor at each setting under the canonical recipe. Figures 12 and 13 report the result.

The picture is mostly stable but not flat. Train loss, eval KL, and CE utilization are roughly invariant across the sweep — the proxy losses see nearly the same training signal at T=1T=1k as at T=8T=8k under matched compression. Compact MCQ accuracy, however, drops modestly with absolute context length, from ∼84.5%\sim 84.5\% at T=1T=1k to ∼80.4%\sim 80.4\% at T=8T=8k. The per-domain breakdown shows the same pattern without a single collapsing domain: at T=8T=8k, Code reaches 79.0%79.0\%, while Financial, Gutenberg, and Legal remain at or above 75%75\%. The takeaway is that compact-cache utility at fixed compression ratio is approximately invariant to absolute context length on the proxy losses, with a modest accuracy hit on the harder domains as TT grows. This supports the design decision to train at moderate TT and rely on iterative compaction (§3.4) for longer deployment contexts, rather than scaling TT in training proportionally to the longest deployment length we want to support.

Appendix I Latent Scaling and CE as a Performance Proxy

Figure 14 tests two diagnostics on the cached multidomain latent sweep. First, compact CE improves smoothly with latent count: fitting CEcompact=a​tb\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{compact}}=at^{b} gives b=−0.31b=-0.31 with R2=0.99R^{2}=0.99. This is not enough evidence for a headline scaling-law claim, but it shows that the trained compactors move along a stable quality–capacity curve rather than producing isolated operating points.

Second, compact CE is a strong proxy for held-out MCQ performance in this regime. Across the six latent counts, the four-domain aggregate MCQ accuracy increases monotonically as compact CE decreases, with Pearson correlation −0.994-0.994 and Spearman correlation −1.000-1.000. This supports using CE and KL as training-time model-selection signals for these sweeps, while keeping the conclusion scoped to a single-seed appendix diagnostic on one model and evaluation mixture.

Appendix J Compression-Ratio Cell-Level Comparisons

The Pareto-style figure in §3.1 compresses the per-cell structure of the design-space sweep into a single frontier; this appendix reports the cell-level views that support the qualitative claims in the body. Figure 15 is the full per-baseline compression-ratio sweep across context lengths, Table 8 gives the exact values behind the Pareto plot, and Figure 16 is the pair of focused pairwise contrasts against the strongest baselines in each non-Still cell of the design space: Attention Matching (per-context synthesis) on the left and KV-Distill (amortized selection) on the right.

J.1 Targeted KVZip partial comparison

KVZip [Kim et al., 2025] is the closest recent baseline to Still’s deployment regime among the missing neighbors because it scores cache entries before the future user query is known. We therefore ported the core cache-quality path into the same Qwen3-4B MCQ protocol used for Table 8: for each document, KVZip’s context-reconstruction prompt assigns per-layer, per-KV-head token importance scores, and the evaluator retains the top KK original cache rows with direct values and no β\beta correction. This keeps the retained-slot budget matched to the other compact-cache baselines, while avoiding a confound from Still-specific value synthesis.

The port above matches the cache-quality question we need to answer for Still: if a query-agnostic selector is given the same retained-cache budget, does it close the gap? On this subset it does not; Still remains higher in every matched 88k and 1616k cell, and KVZip is only competitive with the selection baselines at low compression. We do not run the full 88k–6464k matrix for three reasons. First, this reference port omits KVZip’s optimized sparse-serving kernels and multi-query serving setup, so a full speed claim would not be a faithful systems reproduction. Second, extending the reference implementation to every context length and every document would consume substantial additional evaluation time while adding little to the paper’s main claim, so we report the scoped comparison explicitly and avoid claiming full-matrix dominance over KVZip.

J.2 Prompted summarization baseline

The Summarization baseline in Figure 2, Figure 15, and Table 8 is a two-stage text bottleneck rather than a KV-cache method. For each document and compression budget KK, we first ask Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 to write a natural-language summary with at most KK generated tokens. We then answer the same multiple-choice questions using the generated summary as the only context. The summary generation used temperature 0.70.7, top-p=0.8p=0.8, and top-k=20k=20; the answer pass used temperature 00 and a 16-token cap.

Summarize the following text, providing all key points that might be necessary to answer comprehension questions: {article_text} Summary:

For the answer pass, the model sees Use the provided context to answer the multiple-choice question., followed by the generated summary, the question and answer options, and the instruction Respond with ONLY the answer letter (A, B, C, or D). No explanation.

The compression-ratio sweep makes the structural shape of each baseline’s degradation directly visible. Heuristic selection methods (H2O, SnapKV) and StreamingLLM hold up at moderate compression on shorter contexts, where the retained subset is large enough to carry most of the answer-relevant information, but they degrade smoothly as the budget tightens and as context length grows — the eviction set widens with TT at fixed compression ratio, and the selected subset has to span a longer document with the same number of slots. Amortized selection (KV-Distill) sits above heuristic selection at every comparable cell — the learned scorer is meaningfully better than attention-mass thresholding — but the curves have the same shape: at extreme compression on long context, no choice of original-token subset preserves enough information to recover full-context behavior. Prompted summarization gives the model an answerable text representation and often stays above heuristic selection, but it is slow and discards details before the answer pass. Attention Matching’s curve has a different character. AM is competitive or better than Still at low compression on short contexts, but its degradation steepens sharply once compression and context length push the compact cache into the regime where per-context fitting cannot route enough distributed information through a small number of compact key rows. Still’s curves are the flattest among the full-matrix compact-context methods, with the targeted KVZip check in Appendix J.1 following the same selection-bound pattern on 88k and 1616k.

The Still-vs-AM panel (Figure 16, left) shows the gap small in the upper-left corner and growing with both compression ratio and context length, peaking in the 1616k–3232k columns at extreme compression: at 8×8\times on 88k the gap is roughly a single accuracy point in Still’s favor, and by 32×32\times on 1616k it reaches 42.842.8 points (Still 59.3%59.3\% vs AM 16.5%16.5\%). The cleanest evidence that AM is hitting a representational ceiling rather than a budget-bound failure sits in the 1616k column at high compression, where AM falls to 6.8%6.8\% at 200×200\times, 9.2%9.2\% at 100×100\times, and 12.2%12.2\% at 50×50\times — well below the 21.2%21.2\% no-context floor for that context — while Still stays at 50.5%50.5\%, 51.5%51.5\%, and 53.6%53.6\% in the same cells. The Still-vs-KV-Distill panel has a different shape. At low compression the gap is large in Still’s favor — KV-Distill’s selected subset cannot recover Still’s compact-cache accuracy in those cells — but at higher compression KV-Distill closes most of the gap, and in three cells crosses into a small positive lead, where its scorer’s choice of retained tokens uses the available budget about as well as Still’s compactor.

This is the cell-level evidence behind the §3.1 claim that AM’s degradation is structural rather than budgetary. AM’s per-context optimization is well-conditioned and computationally cheap at extreme compression — the linear systems it solves shrink with KK — so its falloff is not driven by running out of fitting budget. The mechanism is closer to a representational ceiling: the compact cache is geometrically the same as Still’s, but AM’s per-context fitting cannot route enough of a long context’s distributed information through a small number of compact key rows for the frozen base model to recover the original answer distribution. Still uses the same compact-cache geometry but learns to use it across a training distribution, and the resulting compactor synthesizes compact entries that AM’s per-context objective leaves on the table.

The qualitative picture from Figure 2 is that selection-based methods (heuristic and amortized alike) exhibit budget-bound rather than representation-bound degradation, with the breakdown point depending primarily on context length: at short context the selected subset can carry most of the answer-relevant information, and at long context no subset of the original tokens does. This is structurally different from AM’s representational ceiling and from Still’s graceful degradation. Table 9 summarizes the Still–KV-Distill cells that anchor the amortized synthesis versus amortized selection comparison.

Appendix K LongBench Generation Methodology

The LongBench generation audit in Table 2 uses LongBench v1 [Bai et al., 2024a] GovReport and QMSum, evaluated with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. We construct a fresh held-out 16k sample with seed 123123: for each task, we shuffle rows by stable LongBench ID and keep 250250 examples whose context is at least 81928192 Qwen tokens and shorter than 1638416384 tokens (500 examples total). The same sampled manifest is used for Still and KV-Distill. GovReport uses the standard “write a one-page summary” prompt; QMSum uses the transcript plus query prompt. For compact-cache conditions, the prompt prefix and document context are prefetched and compacted, while the post-context task suffix remains on the uncompressed answer path.

Both methods use the same retained budget, K=1024K=1024, the same base model, and the identical generation-aligned continuation recipe. The Still and KV-Distill generation-aligned checkpoints are each short continuations of their respective 16k, K=1024K=1024 checkpoints on GovReport/QMSum summary rows: each retains the top-200200 KL term against the uncompressed-cache teacher and adds answer-text cross-entropy on the reference summaries with weight 100100 for 5050 additional steps. Decoding is deterministic greedy generation with max_new_tokens=192, repetition penalty 1.21.2, and no-repeat 44-gram blocking.

We judge only the Still-vs-KV-Distill pair. For each example, the two outputs are anonymized and randomly assigned to output aliases before judging. The judge is openai/gpt-5.5; it sees the LongBench task input, the reference answer(s), and the anonymized candidate outputs, assigns each output a 00–100100 quality score for factual coverage, faithfulness, and task usefulness, and chooses the better output or a tie. No ties occur in the reported 500500 examples.

Appendix L Long-Context Evaluation Datasets

All long-context evaluations use the Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 tokenizer and record source revisions, tokenizer metadata, seeds, build commands, and row counts in dataset manifests. Table 10 summarizes the four dataset families used for the 32k–128k evaluations. Long-MCQ is the four-domain generated-MCQ suite used for the iterative-compaction headline; the other three datasets stress complementary behaviors: concatenated real reading comprehension, synthetic long-context retrieval and aggregation, and exact needle retrieval.

Appendix M Architecture Ablations

We probe the sensitivity of Still to small architectural choices under a β\beta-enabled diagnostic configuration (distinct from the β=0\beta=0 setup of every reported Still result in the main paper; see Appendix A): Qwen3-4B, 81928192-token context, 10241024 latents (8×8\times compression), dℓ=256d_{\ell}=256, two blocks, repeated cross-attention, RoPE-fix, freely learned β\beta, and answer-token KL training. Each row in Table 11 is trained on the same four-domain MCQ corpus with the same optimizer and schedule; values are tail-means over the final 30%30\% of evaluation checkpoints. The resmse row is an objective diagnostic under the same architecture, not an architecture ablation.

The KL-trained architecture rows are tightly clustered: aggregate MCQ accuracy ranges from 0.7080.708 to 0.7560.756, and eval KL varies by only ∼0.02\sim 0.02 absolute. Removing self-attention, replacing it with an MLP, doubling cross-attention heads, and halving depth all leave Still in the same operating regime. We keep the two-block self-attention configuration for consistency across the main compression sweep, not because this 8×8\times ablation identifies it as load-bearing.

The objective diagnostic separates extractive accuracy from distributional matching. resmse ties the best MCQ accuracy (0.7560.756), but its eval KL and CE are roughly three times worse than the KL-trained rows, and CE utilization falls to 0.4370.437. Direct cache-style objectives can preserve enough content for MCQ answering while producing a compact cache whose output distribution is much farther from the full-context teacher, so we keep KL as the paper-facing objective.

M.1 No inter-layer compactor channel

The per-layer compactors share no information at forward time. We do not add a compactor residual stream between layers because the base model’s residual stream already propagates content vertically: layer ℓ+1\ell+1’s cache is computed from a residual stream that incorporates layer ℓ\ell’s output, so an explicit inter-layer connection would largely duplicate that signal. The architectural ablations above support this — removing self-attention, replacing it with an MLP, doubling cross-attention heads, or halving depth all leave headline metrics in the same operating regime at 8×8\times compression. Adding inter-compactor capacity would also serialize an otherwise embarrassingly parallel forward pass across LL layers, regressing on the speed dimension central to this work.

M.2 Sweeping β\beta

The mass-matched correction βi=β^i+log⁡(T/t)\beta_{i}=\hat{\beta}_{i}+\log(T/t) that Attention Matching uses, and that Still inherits as an optional prior on its bias output (Appendix A), is calibrated for single-pass compaction at a fixed compression ratio T/tT/t. Under iterative chunked compaction (§2.3) the effective ratio grows linearly in the number of passes, so the natural question is whether the same logarithmic correction transfers. We emphasize up front that this subsection is a diagnostic on a β\beta-re-enabled inference path: the headline iterative results in §3.4 all use β=0\beta=0, consistent with every other reported Still configuration in the paper (Appendix A). Here we re-enable the optional bias head on the same canonical 11k/128128-latent checkpoint to ask how much calibration headroom β\beta would buy under recurrence if a deployment supported it. We absorb an 88k context in eight 11k chunks, scaling the correction as βi=β^i+α​log⁡(chunks)\beta_{i}=\hat{\beta}_{i}+\alpha\log(\text{chunks}) for α∈[0,1.25]\alpha\in[0,1.25], and track CE utilization per domain (Figure 17).

The optimum sits at α≈0.5\alpha\approx 0.5 across all four domains; α=1.25\alpha=1.25 collapses utilization in three of the four. The log⁡(chunks)\log(\text{chunks}) form is the right shape but the magnitude required at deployment is roughly half what the single-pass theory prescribes: α=0\alpha=0 underweights the bias and the cache attends too uniformly, α=1\alpha=1 overweights it and attention sharpens past the optimum. The most plausible reading is that the compactor’s own β^i\hat{\beta}_{i} partially absorbs mass-matching across passes, leaving the explicit additive correction redundant by half. The α≈0.5\alpha\approx 0.5 optimum is what re-enabling β\beta would buy at deployment; the reported iterative results in §3.4 sit at β=0\beta=0 throughout, consistent with every other Still number in the paper, so the gap to the per-domain optima here is calibration headroom we leave on the table by choosing not to take a deployment-incompatible dependency on the bias channel. This α\alpha knob is precisely the deployment-time calibration that §5 flags as motivation for training Still directly under the iterative recurrence: a compactor trained against its own compact-cache outputs would absorb the correction into β^i\hat{\beta}_{i} and remove the only deployment-tunable parameter in the system.

M.3 Keys, values, and bias factorization

This diagnostic enables the optional bias head and jointly produces compact keys CkC_{k}, compact values CvC_{v}, and per-token attention biases β\beta. It asks which of the three learned outputs carries the quality gain. If selected keys plus synthesized values are nearly sufficient, then the main benefit of Still is value synthesis on top of ordinary token routing. If learned keys are also necessary, then the compactor is not merely filling selected memory slots with better content; it is learning the routing structure of the compact cache itself.

Setup.

We train six Qwen3-4B compactors at three compression regimes, 8192→10248192\rightarrow 1024 (8×8\times), 8192→1288192\rightarrow 128 (64×64\times), and 8192→418192\rightarrow 41 (200×200\times), holding the dataset, optimizer, training budget, and evaluation protocol fixed. We report the matched step-1500 checkpoint for each run. The beta-enabled baseline learns CkC_{k}, CvC_{v}, and β\beta. The remaining variants ablate one part of this factorization: remove β\beta entirely; replace learned β\beta with the constant log⁡(T/t)\log(T/t); use learned keys but selected values; use selected keys but learned values; or learn values only with selected keys and uniform β\beta. In the selected-key/value variants, selected entries are the top-kk source positions by key RMS, so the comparison is deliberately against a simple query-independent selection rule rather than a tuned retrieval baseline.

Results.

Figure 18 shows that the learned bias is not the main source of the gain at low or medium compression. At 8×8\times, β\beta-enabled Still reaches 76.5%76.5\% compact MCQ accuracy and eval KL 0.2910.291; no-β\beta and fixed-β\beta are essentially tied at 74.0%/0.29174.0\%/0.291 and 76.0%/0.28776.0\%/0.287. At 64×64\times, the same pattern holds: β\beta-enabled Still reaches 48.0%48.0\% and KL 0.5560.556, no-β\beta reaches 48.0%/0.55348.0\%/0.553, and fixed-β\beta reaches 51.0%/0.56151.0\%/0.561. At the extreme 200×200\times point, learned β\beta matters more for MCQ answer generation: β\beta-enabled Still reaches 50.5%50.5\% compact accuracy, compared with 39.0%39.0\% for no-β\beta and 47.0%47.0\% for fixed-β\beta, while the KL proxy remains close for all three (0.5960.596, 0.5950.595, and 0.6100.610).

Both learned keys and learned values matter.

The selection hybrids are the informative rows. Learned keys with selected values is consistently weak, reaching only 36.0%36.0\% at 8×8\times, 36.0%36.0\% at 64×64\times, and 31.0%31.0\% at 200×200\times. Selected keys with learned values recovers part of the gap (49.0%49.0\%, 42.0%42.0\%, and 36.0%36.0\%), and learned-values-only lands in the same lower band (42.0%42.0\%, 44.0%44.0\%, and 39.0%39.0\%), but all remain well below β\beta-enabled Still at the matched ratios. These results support the interpretation that values carry much of the recoverable content, but learned keys are not dispensable: synthesized values help when routed through selected keys, yet the best compact cache requires learning the router and the content jointly. Still’s advantage is not only that it writes better values into a selected memory; it also learns compact keys that organize how the frozen model will retrieve from that memory.

Appendix O Iterative Compaction

This appendix reports the full iterative-compaction diagnostics. The main paper focuses on Long-MCQ because it gives the cleanest long-context signal: the same benchmark has stable full-context and no-context references at 32k/64k/128k, and the 16k- and 32k-trained compactors remain useful at 128k. The appendix includes the broader aggregate sweep, QuALITY transfer, RULER transfer, task-level RULER breakdowns, per-domain Long-MCQ results, and an evaluation-mode ablation.

The aggregate sweep in Figure 19 collects the earlier context-sweep evaluations into one view. It is useful as a sanity check but less clean than the Long-MCQ result because it mixes evaluation surfaces and context ranges. The qualitative conclusion is consistent: models trained only for short iterative horizons can look strong at 8k and 16k, but the ordering changes at longer contexts.

Figure 20 shows that QuALITY is more brittle under repeated compaction than Long-MCQ. The dual-path answer-only run is the best short-context result, reaching about 60% at 8k and 59% at 16k, but it drops to roughly the no-context floor at 32k. The 16k and 32k rationale runs are more stable but lower overall. This supports two conclusions: prompt surface matters for iterative compaction, and long-context QuALITY should be used as a diagnostic rather than as the central online result.

RULER exposes the main weakness of the current iterative setup (Figure 21). The best aggregate 32k result is the 16k-trained lookahead compactor at 33.8%, followed by the 32k-trained lookahead compactor at 29.5%. At 64k these fall to 18.1% and 17.6%. Dual-path and true two-stage variants help on some individual tasks but do not close the aggregate gap. We therefore report RULER as a diagnostic of what remains difficult: repeated compaction can preserve broad MCQ evidence, but exact synthetic retrieval and position-sensitive tasks are not solved by the current training recipe.

The task heatmap in Figure 22 explains the aggregate RULER behavior. The model can retain some structured evidence: CWE reaches 90.0% at 32k, FWE reaches 73.3%, and QA/VT tasks remain above zero. The needle tasks are different. Both single-needle and multi-key needle variants are near zero at 32k and 64k. This suggests that the current iterative compactor is not reliably preserving exact token strings through many compression events, even when it retains enough semantic information for less brittle tasks.

Figure 23 breaks the Long-MCQ result down by domain. The 16k-trained compactor is strongest on Financial at 64k (64.0%) and remains nontrivial on Code, Financial, and Gutenberg at 128k. The 32k-trained compactor is more balanced at 128k, reaching 45.0% on Code, 41.0% on Financial, 36.0% on Gutenberg, and 35.0% on Legal. The domain view supports the main claim: the long-context result is distributed across domains rather than driven by one easy subset.

The ablation in Figure 24 motivates the curated main figure. Single-stage lookahead compactors trained at matched or near-matched horizons are the most reliable family. No-lookahead retains useful short-context performance but is less stable at long contexts. Concat-final and true two-stage variants are useful engineering diagnostics, but they do not improve the aggregate long-context result. This is why the main figure reports the simple 8k/16k/32k lookahead ladder: it isolates the effect of training horizon without mixing in secondary evaluation-mode changes.

Appendix P Broader Impacts

Still is a systems method for reducing the retained KV cache of frozen language models. Potential positive impacts include lower memory cost, lower serving cost, and broader access to long-context inference on constrained hardware. Potential negative impacts follow from making long-context language-model deployment cheaper and more capable: the same efficiency gains could lower the cost of harmful automation, surveillance over long records, or generation systems that process sensitive documents. Still does not add new generative capabilities to the base model, but responsible deployment should inherit the base model’s safety, privacy, and access-control safeguards and should treat compacted caches as sensitive derived model state.
